claims.evidence: This is a description of the model construction.

claims.claim: Two SPBs are embedded in the nuclear envelope but free to move on the surface of the sphere.
claims.source: Two SPBs are embedded in the nuclear envelope but free to move on the surface of the sphere (although we also consider effects of allowing SPBs to move radially due to a soft nuclear envelope in one variant of the model, as discussed below).
claims.evidence: This is a description of the model construction.

claims.claim: Each SPB nucleates 14 MTs, with their minus-ends tethered to the SPBs by a spring and which undergo dynamic instability at their plus-ends.
claims.source: Each SPB nucleates 14 MTs, with their minus-ends tethered to the SPBs by a spring and which undergo dynamic instability at their plus-ends.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the model construction.

claims.claim: Kinesin-5 motors move bidirectionally on MTs.
claims.source: Kinesin-5 motors (representing Cut7) move bidirectionally on MTs (Edamatsu, 2014; Edamatsu, 2016; Britto et al., 2016; Singh et al., 2018), with plus-end directed movement on antiparallel MTs exerting force to slide apart the SPBs.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature on kinesin-5 motor behavior.

claims.claim: Kinesin-5 motors exert force to slide apart the SPBs with plus-end directed movement on antiparallel MTs.
claims.source: Kinesin-5 motors (representing Cut7) move bidirectionally on MTs (Edamatsu, 2014; Edamatsu, 2016; Britto et al., 2016; Singh et al., 2018), with plus-end directed movement on antiparallel MTs exerting force to slide apart the SPBs.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature and is part of the model construction.

claims.claim: Kinesin-14 motors crosslink MTs and one head walks toward the MT minus-ends, aligning MTs and exerting force that shortens the spindle.
claims.source: Kinesin-14 motors (representing Pkl1 and Klp2) crosslink MTs and one head walks toward the MT minus-ends, aligning MTs and exerting force that shortens the spindle (Pidoux et al., 1996; Troxell et al., 2001; Chen et al., 2012; Olmsted et al., 2014; Hepperla et al., 2014; Yukawa et al., 2015; Yukawa et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature on kinesin-14 motor behavior.

claims.claim: Crosslinkers preferentially bind antiparallel MTs.
claims.source: Crosslinkers (representing Ase1) preferentially bind antiparallel MTs (Yamashita et al., 2005; Loïodice et al., 2005; Janson et al., 2007; Kapitein et al., 2008; Courtheoux et al., 2009; Fu et al., 2009) and stabilize MT overlaps when crosslinking near the end of an MT, an effect which mimics the recruitment of stabilizing proteins such as CLASP (Bratman and Chang, 2007) to MT ends.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature on crosslinker behavior.

claims.claim: Crosslinkers stabilize MT overlaps when crosslinking near the end of an MT, an effect which mimics the recruitment of stabilizing proteins such as CLASP to MT ends.
claims.source: Crosslinkers (representing Ase1) preferentially bind antiparallel MTs (Yamashita et al., 2005; Loïodice et al., 2005; Janson et al., 2007; Kapitein et al., 2008; Courtheoux et al., 2009; Fu et al., 2009) and stabilize MT overlaps when crosslinking near the end of an MT, an effect which mimics the recruitment of stabilizing proteins such as CLASP (Bratman and Chang, 2007) to MT ends.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature and is part of the model construction.

claims.claim: Fission-yeast kinetochores can bind up to 3 MTs.
claims.source: Because fission-yeast kinetochores can bind up to 3 MTs (Ding et al., 1993), each kinetochore has three attachment factors in the model separated by 40 nm along the kinetochore plate (Figure 1C, Appendix 1—figure 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature on kinetochore structure.

claims.claim: Attachment factors can make both lateral and end-on attachments to MTs, with different binding kinetics that favor end-on attachment.
claims.source: Attachment factors can make both lateral and end-on attachments to MTs, with different binding kinetics that favor end-on attachment.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the model construction.

claims.claim: The model includes tip tracking: a tip-bound attachment factor tracks MT ends by maintaining end-on attachment during MT growth and shrinking.
claims.source: Importantly, the model includes tip tracking: a tip-bound attachment factor tracks MT ends by maintaining end-on attachment during MT growth and shrinking.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the model construction.

claims.claim: End-on attachment alters MT dynamic instability and is force-dependent, as measured previously.
claims.source: End-on attachment alters MT dynamic instability and is force-dependent, as measured previously (Akiyoshi et al., 2010; Miller et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature on kinetochore-MT attachment.

claims.claim: Sister kinetochores are linked via springs that resist stretching and rotation, to maintain the distance and alignment of the kinetochores.
claims.source: Sister kinetochores are linked via springs that resist stretching and rotation, to maintain the distance and alignment of the kinetochores (Figure 1C, Appendix 1—figure 1; Mary et al., 2015; Smith et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature and is part of the model construction.

claims.claim: The pericentric DNA is modeled as a spherocylinder of length 200 nm and diameter 75 nm, which has a soft repulsion with MTs that allows MT-chromatin overlap with an energy penalty.
claims.source: The pericentric DNA is modeled as a spherocylinder of length 200 nm and diameter 75 nm, which has a soft repulsion with MTs that allows MT-chromatin overlap with an energy penalty (Appendix 1).
claims.evidence: This is a description of the model construction.

claims.claim: The model can achieve both correct and erroneous kinetochore-MT attachment states.
claims.source: With these ingredients, the model can achieve both correct and erroneous kinetochore-MT attachment states (Figure 1D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 1D.

claims.claim: Three key model ingredients were required to achieve error correction and persistent biorientation: progressive restriction of attachment, destabilization of misaligned attachment, and stabilization of attachment by force.
claims.source: To achieve error correction and persistent biorientation, we found three key model ingredients were required: progressive restriction of attachment (Figure 1E), destabilization of misaligned attachment (Figure 1F), and stabilization of attachment by force (Figure 1G, Appendix 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results showing the necessity of these three mechanisms.

claims.claim: The model exhibits both spindle assembly and chromosome biorientation.
claims.source: With these mechanisms, the model exhibits both spindle assembly and chromosome biorientation (Figure 1H, Video 1).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 1H and Video 1.

claims.claim: Simulations of the reference model showed dynamics of SPB separation, kinetochore movement along the spindle, and interkinetochore stretch similar to the experimental data.
claims.source: After refinement, simulations of the reference model showed dynamics of SPB separation, kinetochore movement along the spindle, and interkinetochore stretch similar to the experimental data (Figure 2E–H, Video 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of simulation results to experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claims.claim: Kinesin-5 motors are essential for spindle assembly in S. pombe.
claims.source: Kinesin-5 motors are essential for spindle assembly in S. pombe, and temperature-sensitive mutants of the kinesin-5/Cut7 fail to separate spindle-pole bodies (Hagan and Yanagida, 1990; Hagan and Yanagida, 1992; Yukawa et al., 2018; Toda et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature on kinesin-5 function.

claims.claim: Temperature-sensitive mutants of the kinesin-5/Cut7 fail to separate spindle-pole bodies.
claims.source: Kinesin-5 motors are essential for spindle assembly in S. pombe, and temperature-sensitive mutants of the kinesin-5/Cut7 fail to separate spindle-pole bodies (Hagan and Yanagida, 1990; Hagan and Yanagida, 1992; Yukawa et al., 2018; Toda et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature on kinesin-5 mutants.

claims.claim: When kinesin-5 is removed from the model, SPBs do not separate.
claims.source: Consistent with this, when we remove kinesin-5 from the model, SPBs do not separate (Figure 2J).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 2J.

claims.claim: The microtubule-associated protein CLASP is essential for spindle assembly in fission yeast, where it is recruited to MT antiparallel overlaps by Ase1 and stabilizes MT dynamics.
claims.source: Similarly, the microtubule-associated protein CLASP is essential for spindle assembly in fission yeast, where it is recruited to MT antiparallel overlaps by Ase1 and stabilizes MT dynamics (Bratman and Chang, 2007).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature on CLASP function.

claims.claim: When the stabilization of dynamics of crosslinked MTs is turned off in the model, SPBs do not separate.
claims.source: When the stabilization of dynamics of crosslinked MTs is turned off in the model, SPBs do not separate (Figure 2K).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 2K.

claims.claim: Chromosome biorientation is abolished in models where the SPBs do not separate.
claims.source: Chromosome biorientation is abolished in models where the SPBs do not separate (Figure 2L, Video 2).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 2L and Video 2.

claims.claim: Cells lacking Klp2 or both Pkl1 and Klp2 do not show altered average spindle length.
claims.source: Experimentally, cells lacking Klp2 or both Pkl1 and Klp2 do not show altered average spindle length (Syrovatkina et al., 2013; Troxell et al., 2001).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature on kinesin-14 mutants.

claims.claim: Model spindles formed and bioriented chromosomes in the absence of kinesin-14, and spindle length depended on the ratio of kinesin-5 to crosslinkers.
claims.source: Consistent with this, model spindles formed and bioriented chromosomes in the absence of kinesin-14, and spindle length depended on the ratio of kinesin-5 to crosslinkers.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results.

claims.claim: Ase1 deletion cells assemble spindles in fission yeast.
claims.source: In fission yeast, Ase1 deletion cells assemble spindles (Yamashita et al., 2005; Syrovatkina et al., 2013; Yukawa et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature on Ase1 deletion.

claims.claim: Removing crosslinkers in the reference model abolished spindle assembly because spindles cannot maintain robust antiparallel MT overlaps.
claims.source: Removing crosslinkers in the reference model abolished spindle assembly because spindles cannot maintain robust antiparallel MT overlaps.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results.

claims.claim: In the reference model the kinesin-14 motors are highly sensitive to force-dependent unbinding: the characteristic distance that quantifies this is 3.2 times larger for kinesin-14 motors than kinesin-5 motors.
claims.source: However, in the reference model the kinesin-14 motors are highly sensitive to force-dependent unbinding: the characteristic distance that quantifies this is 3.2 times larger for kinesin-14 motors than kinesin-5 motors.
claims.evidence: This is a description of the model parameters.

claims.claim: When kinesin-14 motors are modeled with the same force sensitivity to unbinding as for the kinesin-5 motors, spindle formation and chromosome biorientation are rescued.
claims.source: When we model the kinesin-14 motors with the same force sensitivity to unbinding as for the kinesin-5 motors, spindle formation and chromosome biorientation are rescued (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: A soft nuclear envelope leads to slightly longer spindles.
claims.source: The results show that a soft nuclear envelope leads to slightly longer spindles (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D, Video 3), but for a physically realistic nuclear envelope force of around 17 pN, spindle length remains near 3 μm, as measured experimentally.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D and Video 3.

claims.claim: For a physically realistic nuclear envelope force of around 17 pN, spindle length remains near 3 μm, as measured experimentally.
claims.source: The results show that a soft nuclear envelope leads to slightly longer spindles (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D, Video 3), but for a physically realistic nuclear envelope force of around 17 pN, spindle length remains near 3 μm, as measured experimentally.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of simulation results to experimental measurements.

claims.claim: Biorientation requires the model to correct attachment errors and maintain correct attachments.
claims.source: Biorientation requires the model to correct attachment errors and maintain correct attachments.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the simulation results.

claims.claim: Biorientation occurs in the simulations primarily through progressive restriction of attachment angle, misaligned destabilization, and force-dependent kinetochore-MT attachment.
claims.source: This occurs in the simulations primarily through progressive restriction of attachment angle, misaligned destabilization, and force-dependent kinetochore-MT attachment.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results showing the importance of these three mechanisms.

claims.claim: The model progressively restricts the angle at which binding can occur as more MTs bind to facilitate correct initial attachment of MTs to kinetochores.
claims.source: To facilitate correct initial attachment of MTs to kinetochores, the model progressively restricts the angle at which binding can occur as more MTs bind (Figure 1E).
claims.evidence: This is a description of the model construction.

claims.claim: Progressive restriction is motivated by previous work demonstrating that kinetochore geometry and chromosome rotation play an important role in promoting correct kinetochore-MT attachment and correcting errors.
claims.source: This is motivated by previous work demonstrating that kinetochore geometry and chromosome rotation play an important role in promoting correct kinetochore-MT attachment and correcting errors (Gregan et al., 2007; Rumpf et al., 2010; Paul et al., 2009; Magidson et al., 2015; Zaytsev and Grishchuk, 2015).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature on kinetochore geometry and error correction.

claims.claim: Unattached kinetochores have a wide angular range over which attachments can form.
claims.source: In our model, unattached kinetochores have a wide angular range over which attachments can form (modeled as an angular spring constant for binding, represented by the three wide cones in Figure 1E left).
claims.evidence: This is a description of the model construction.

claims.claim: Each attachment formed narrows the angle allowed for the subsequent attachment, favoring attachment to MTs that are more perpendicular to the kinetochore plate.
claims.source: Each attachment formed narrows the angle allowed for the subsequent attachment, favoring attachment to MTs that are more perpendicular to the kinetochore plate (represented by the narrower cones in Figure 1E right).
claims.evidence: This is a description of the model construction.

claims.claim: When attachment angle is most permissive, merotelic attachments form and are not corrected sufficiently rapidly to biorient the chromosomes.
claims.source: These failures occur for different reasons as the angular spring constant varies. When attachment angle is most permissive, merotelic attachments form and are not corrected sufficiently rapidly to biorient the chromosomes.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results.

claims.claim: When the attachment angle is highly restricted, attachments are unlikely to form at all.
claims.source: When the attachment angle is highly restricted, attachments are unlikely to form at all.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results.

claims.claim: Progressive restriction of attachment is essential for biorientation in the model.
claims.source: Overall, this result shows that in our model progressive restriction of attachment is essential for biorientation.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results showing that removing progressive restriction abolishes biorientation.

claims.claim: For the first attachment, promoting kinetochore binding to any MT is important: initial attachments should be established easily, even if erroneous.
claims.source: This means that for the first attachment, promoting kinetochore binding to any MT is important: initial attachments should be established easily, even if erroneous.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the simulation results.

claims.claim: Biorientation is increased when the third (final) binding event is highly restricted.
claims.source: By contrast, biorientation is increased when the third (final) binding event is highly restricted (Figure 3C): chromosomes are bioriented in the model <10% of the time when the third attachment is most permissive, but the fraction of simultaneous biorientation increases with the angular stiffness of the third binding site.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: The second value of the angular potential for progressive restriction was less important.
claims.source: The second value of the angular potential for progressive restriction was less important (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A): varying it did not significantly change the fraction of simultaneous biorientation.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: Varying the number of allowed kinetochore-MT attachments does not significantly affect how easily biorientation is achieved.
claims.source: Because of the importance of progressive restriction in our model, we additionally examined whether varying the number of allowed kinetochore-MT attachments might affect how easily biorientation is achieved, but found no significant effect (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: Merotelic attachments are common in early mitosis and are corrected over time.
claims.source: Previous experimental work has shown that merotelic attachments are common in early mitosis and are corrected over time (Cimini et al., 2003) due to increased turnover of kinetochore MTs from the activity of Aurora B kinase (DeLuca et al., 2006; Cimini et al., 2006; Gay et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature on merotelic attachments and error correction.

claims.claim: Merotelic attachments are corrected over time due to increased turnover of kinetochore MTs from the activity of Aurora B kinase.
claims.source: Previous experimental work has shown that merotelic attachments are common in early mitosis and are corrected over time (Cimini et al., 2003) due to increased turnover of kinetochore MTs from the activity of Aurora B kinase (DeLuca et al., 2006; Cimini et al., 2006; Gay et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature on Aurora B kinase function.

claims.claim: Experimental work has demonstrated a decrease in kinetochore MT turnover by up to a factor of 65 in the presence of Aurora B inhibitors.
claims.source: Because experimental work has demonstrated a decrease in kinetochore MT turnover by up to a factor of 65 in the presence of Aurora B inhibitors (Cimini et al., 2006), we varied the misaligned destabilization factor in the model, which quantifies the increased turnover of incorrect attachments, over a similar range from 1 to 100 (Figure 3D, Video 4).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature on Aurora B inhibitors.

claims.claim: Biorientation is nearly eliminated in the absence of misaligned destabilization.
claims.source: Consistent with experimental results, biorientation is nearly eliminated in the absence of misaligned destabilization.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results.

claims.claim: Biorientation time in the model is maximum when the misaligned destabilization factor is 70, comparable to the experimental value.
claims.source: Biorientation time in the model is maximum when the misaligned destabilization factor is 70, comparable to the experimental value.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results and comparison to experimental values.

claims.claim: Misaligned destabilization demonstrates the importance of error correction in the model.
claims.source: This demonstrates the importance of error correction in the model.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the simulation results.

claims.claim: Kinetochore-MT attachments are stabilized by force.
claims.source: We therefore additionally tested a force-dependent error correction model, based on previous results that kinetochore-MT attachments are stabilized by force (Nicklas and Koch, 1969; Cane et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature on force-dependent attachment.

claims.claim: The force-stabilization model of error correction experiences the initial problem of biorientation (IPBO): a bioriented attachment that has just formed is not under tension, and therefore is not stable.
claims.source: The force-stabilization model of error correction that we implemented experiences the initial problem of biorientation (IPBO): a bioriented attachment that has just formed is not under tension, and therefore is not stable (Zhang et al., 2013; Kalantzaki et al., 2015; Tubman et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature on the IPBO and is an inference from the model construction.

claims.claim: Implementing force-dependent stabilization alone did not lead to biorientation.
claims.source: Consistent with this, we found implementing force-dependent stabilization alone did not lead to biorientation.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results.

claims.claim: The IPBO may be solved by initial syntelic-like attachments that are end-on between the kinetochore face near a pole, and lateral to the kinetochore farther from that same pole.
claims.source: Recent work has suggested that the IPBO may be solved by initial syntelic-like attachments that are end-on between the kinetochore face near a pole, and lateral to the kinetochore farther from that same pole (Kuhn and Dumont, 2017).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature on solving the IPBO.

claims.claim: Long-lived biorientation was achieved in the force-dependent error correction model with model parameters that favored end-on over lateral attachments, inhibited attachments at high angle, and allowed sister kinetochores to more easily reorient.
claims.source: We were able to achieve long-lived biorientation in the force-dependent error correction model with model parameters that favored end-on over lateral attachments, inhibited attachments at high angle, and allowed sister kinetochores to more easily reorient (Table 6).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results.

claims.claim: The model is sensitive to the value of the characteristic force that controls how much attachments are stabilized by force, with best performance of the model at a characteristic force of 1.67 pN.
claims.source: We found that the model is sensitive to the value of this characteristic force, with best performance of the model at a characteristic force of 1.67 pN.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results.

claims.claim: Higher or lower values of the characteristic force decrease cumulative biorientation by up to a factor of two.
claims.source: Higher or lower values decrease cumulative biorientation by up to a factor of two.
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results.

claims.claim: Attachments between single MTs and purified budding-yeast kinetochores were altered by force applied to the kinetochore, even in the absence of Aurora kinase.
claims.source: Attachments between single MTs and purified budding-yeast kinetochores were altered by force applied to the kinetochore, even in the absence of Aurora kinase (Akiyoshi et al., 2010; Miller et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature on force-dependent attachment.

claims.claim: The kinetochore-MT attachment lifetime increased with tension when kinetochores were attached to depolymerizing MTs, an effect dependent on a TOG protein.
claims.source: In particular, the kinetochore-MT attachment lifetime increased with tension when kinetochores were attached to depolymerizing MTs, an effect dependent on a TOG protein (Akiyoshi et al., 2010; Miller et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature on force-dependent attachment.

claims.claim: Force dependence of attachments is required to maintain biorientation in the model.
claims.source: Consistent with this, we implemented force dependence of attachments in the model (Figure 1G). This effect is required to maintain biorientation: if we eliminate the force dependence of attachment kinetics, biorientation is nearly abolished in the model (Figure 3F, Video 4).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 3F and Video 4.

claims.claim: The increase in attachment lifetime of a kinetochore bound to a shrinking MT is the key force-dependent rate for maintaining biorientation.
claims.source: To understand which force-dependent rate is most important for this effect, we added them back to the model one at a time. The increase in attachment lifetime of a kinetochore bound to a shrinking MT is the key force-dependent rate, because making this the only force-dependent lifetime in the model restores nearly all biorientation compared to the model with all rates force-dependent (Figure 3F).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 3F.

claims.claim: Maintenance of biorientation requires kinetochore-MT attachments to persist during MT depolymerization.
claims.source: This demonstrates that maintenance of biorientation requires kinetochore-MT attachments to persist during MT depolymerization.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the simulation results.

claims.claim: One key determinant of the magnitude of spindle length fluctuations is the lifetime of kinetochore-MT attachments.
claims.source: One key determinant of the magnitude of spindle length fluctuations is the lifetime of kinetochore-MT attachments (Figure 4, Video 6).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 4 and Video 6.

claims.claim: The magnitude of length fluctuations increases with kinetochore-MT attachment lifetime: the longer the lifetime, the larger the fluctuations.
claims.source: This measure of length fluctuations increases with kinetochore-MT attachment lifetime: the longer the lifetime, the larger the fluctuations (Figure 4A–D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 4A–D.

claims.claim: For long-lived attachment, the force exerted by a stretched kinetochore can grow over time to a larger value: long-lived attachment allows multiple MTs to bind per kinetochore, exert greater force, and stretch apart the sisters.
claims.source: To understand this result, note that for long-lived attachment, the force exerted by a stretched kinetochore can grow over time to a larger value: long-lived attachment allows multiple MTs to bind per kinetochore, exert greater force, and stretch apart the sisters.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the simulation results.

claims.claim: The average interkinetochore distance increases with kinetochore-MT attachment lifetime.
claims.source: Indeed, the average interkinetochore distance increases with kinetochore-MT attachment lifetime (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by simulation results shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: Slow cycles of attachment and detachment lead to slowly varying force on the spindle that causes its length to fluctuate.
claims.source: Thus, slow cycles of attachment and detachment lead to slowly varying force on the spindle that causes its length to fluctuate.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the simulation results.

claims.claim: Short-lived kinetochore-MT attachment causes relatively quick turnover, limiting interkinetochore stretch, inward force, and variation in inward force.
claims.source: In the opposite limit, short-lived kinetochore-MT attachment causes relatively quick turnover, limiting interkinetochore stretch, inward force, and variation in inward force.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the simulation results.

claims.claim: Altered kinetochore-MT attachment lifetime could be a downstream effect that may result from the diverse mutations observed to cause spindle length fluctuations in S. pombe.
claims.source: This analysis suggests that altered kinetochore-MT attachment lifetime could be a downstream effect that may result from the diverse mutations observed to cause spindle length fluctuations in S. pombe.
claims.evidence: This is speculation based on the simulation results.

claims.claim: The effect of lifetime may not be the only source of spindle length fluctuations: other mutations that lead to slow changes in force exerted on the spindle could have similar effects.
claims.source: We note that the effect of lifetime may not be the only source of spindle length fluctuations: other mutations that lead to slow changes in force exerted on the spindle could have similar effects.
claims.evidence: This is speculation based on the simulation results.

claims.claim: The force-balance model can explain why multiple perturbations alter steady-state spindle length, including mutation of motors and microtubule-associated proteins.
claims.source: The force-balance model can explain why multiple perturbations alter steady-state spindle length, including mutation of motors and microtubule-associated proteins (Syrovatkina et al., 2013; Hepperla et al., 2014), and chromosome/kinetochore number and chromatin stiffness (Chacón et al., 2014; Nannas et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature on spindle length perturbations.

claims.claim: The force-balance model can explain why multiple perturbations alter steady-state spindle length, including chromosome/kinetochore number and chromatin stiffness.
claims.source: The force-balance model can explain why multiple perturbations alter steady-state spindle length, including mutation of motors and microtubule-associated proteins (Syrovatkina et al., 2013; Hepperla et al., 2014), and chromosome/kinetochore number and chromatin stiffness (Chacón et al., 2014; Nannas et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature on spindle length perturbations.

claims.claim: It can be challenging to distinguish direct from indirect effects of altering force balance.
claims.source: However, it can be challenging to distinguish direct from indirect effects of altering force balance.
claims.evidence: This is a general statement about the difficulty of interpreting experimental results.

claims.claim: In budding yeast, kinesin-14 deletion leads to shorter spindles, because kinesin-14 helps bundle spindle MTs, allowing kinesin-5 motors to generate greater outward force when kinesin-14 is present.
claims.source: However, in budding yeast, kinesin-14 deletion instead leads to shorter spindles, because kinesin-14 helps bundle spindle MTs, allowing kinesin-5 motors to generate greater outward force when kinesin-14 is present (Hepperla et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous literature on kinesin-14 function in budding yeast.

claims.claim: Kinesin-8 deletion in fission yeast leads to longer spindles, but this is likely due to effects of this motor on MT dynamics rather than direct inward force generation by kinesin-8.
claims.source: Similarly, kinesin-8 deletion in fission yeast leads to longer spindles, but this is likely due to effects of this motor on MT dynamics rather than direct inward force generation by kinesin-8 (Syrovatkina et al., 2013; Gergely et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature on kinesin-8 function.

claims.claim: For early time (up to 5 min) when spindles are short (up to 1 μm), motors and crosslinkers exert force that slowly increases in magnitude up to a few tens of pN, but chromosomes exert almost no force.
claims.source: For early time (up to 5 min) when spindles are short (up to 1 μm), motors and crosslinkers exert force that slowly increases in magnitude up to a few tens of pN, but chromosomes exert almost no force (Figure 5C,F,I, Video 7).
claims.evidence: This claim is supported by force analysis in the computational model shown in Figure 5C,F,I and Video 7.

claims.claim: Chromosomes do not exert significant inward force during initial SPB separation because they are not bioriented on the spindle.
claims.source: Because chromosomes are not bioriented on the spindle during initial SPB separation, they do not exert significant inward force.
claims.evidence: This is an inference from the simulation results.

claims.claim: Initial bipolar spindle assembly can occur in a model lacking chromosomes.

results.result: The computational model identifies three essential mechanisms for robust chromosome biorientation: progressive restriction of kinetochore-MT attachment geometry, destabilization of misaligned attachments, and force-dependent attachment kinetics.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C3, C28-C30, C55, and C73 collectively demonstrate through computational modeling that all three mechanisms are required for biorientation. The model shows that removing any single mechanism nearly abolishes biorientation (Figures 3A, 3D, 3F), providing strong convergent evidence that these are essential requirements.

results.result: Progressive restriction of kinetochore-MT attachment angle is essential for biorientation, with the first attachment requiring permissive binding and the final attachment requiring highly restricted binding.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C87 demonstrate through systematic parameter variation (Figure 3A-C) that progressive restriction is essential, with specific requirements for each binding event. The model shows biorientation is abolished without progressive restriction and that the first attachment must be permissive while the third must be highly restricted.

results.result: Destabilization of misaligned attachments by approximately 70-fold, mimicking Aurora B kinase activity, is required for error correction and optimal biorientation in the model.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C93 and C152-C153 show through parameter variation (Figure 3D) that a destabilization factor of ~70 gives optimal biorientation, matching experimental measurements of Aurora B effects. Biorientation is nearly eliminated without destabilization, demonstrating its necessity.

results.result: Force-dependent stabilization of kinetochore-MT attachments during microtubule depolymerization is required to maintain biorientation, with optimal performance at a characteristic force of 1.67 pN.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C105 and C154 demonstrate through model perturbations (Figure 3E-F) that force-dependent attachment kinetics are essential, with the key rate being increased lifetime during MT depolymerization. The model shows biorientation is nearly abolished without this mechanism and is sensitive to the characteristic force parameter.

results.result: Long kinetochore-MT attachment lifetime causes large spindle length fluctuations because slow attachment/detachment cycles lead to slowly varying forces on the spindle.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C31-C32, and C106-C113 demonstrate through systematic variation of attachment lifetime (Figure 4) that longer lifetimes correlate with larger spindle length fluctuations. The mechanism is explained by increased interkinetochore stretch with longer lifetimes leading to larger, slowly varying inward forces.

results.result: During early spindle assembly (spindles <1 μm), kinesin-5 motors generate outward force that is opposed by passive crosslinkers generating high braking force on short MT overlaps, with minimal contribution from chromosomes.
results.evaluation: Claims C5, C119-C132, and C161-C163 demonstrate through force analysis (Figure 5C,F,I) that early spindle assembly is dominated by motor and crosslinker forces, with crosslinker force peaking at ~25 pN for 0.75 μm spindles then decreasing. Chromosomes contribute minimal force because they are not yet bioriented.

results.result: After biorientation (spindles >1 μm), interkinetochore stretch becomes the primary inward force balancing kinesin-5 outward force to set metaphase spindle length.
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C133-C139, C164-C165 demonstrate through force analysis (Figure 5C,F,I) that after biorientation, chromosome force becomes significant and balances kinesin-5 force. Perturbations that alter chromosome attachment or MT dynamics correspondingly alter spindle length through changes in interkinetochore stretch.

results.result: The model can robustly segregate chromosomes in anaphase with minimal additional mechanisms beyond those required for biorientation.
results.evaluation: Claims C7, C35, C140-C143, and C166 demonstrate through anaphase simulations (Figure 6) that adding only chromatin spring severing, attachment stabilization, and MT depolymerization enables robust chromosome segregation. Segregation dynamics match experimental measurements, supporting the sufficiency of these mechanisms.

results.result: A 3D computational model of fission yeast mitosis incorporating stochastic binding kinetics, force-dependent dynamics, and biologically-motivated parameters can successfully assemble bipolar spindles and biorient chromosomes from side-by-side centrosomes.
results.evaluation: Claims C27, C36-C54, C56, and C144 describe the model construction and demonstrate its capability (Figure 1H, Video 1). The model incorporates established biophysical principles and achieves both spindle assembly and chromosome biorientation, validating the modeling approach.

results.result: The computational model quantitatively reproduces experimental measurements of spindle dynamics, chromosome movements, and timing in fission yeast.
results.evaluation: Claims C57, C145-C146, and C156 demonstrate through direct comparison (Figure 2E-H) that the model reproduces experimental dynamics of SPB separation, kinetochore movement, and interkinetochore stretch. The timing of spindle assembly and biorientation matches experimental observations.

results.result: Model perturbations recapitulate genetic requirements: removing kinesin-5 or crosslinker-mediated MT stabilization abolishes spindle assembly and chromosome biorientation.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C63 demonstrate through model perturbations (Figure 2J-L) that removing kinesin-5 or MT stabilization prevents SPB separation and abolishes biorientation, matching experimental genetics. This validates that the model captures essential biological requirements.

results.result: The model reproduces the non-essential role of kinesin-14 and the conditional requirement for crosslinkers depending on motor force sensitivity.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C69 show through model perturbations (Figure 2—figure supplement 1) that spindles can form without kinesin-14 (matching experiments) and that crosslinker requirement depends on kinesin-14 force sensitivity. When kinesin-14 force sensitivity is reduced, crosslinkers become dispensable.

results.result: A soft nuclear envelope model produces slightly longer spindles but maintains near-physiological length (~3 μm) at realistic membrane forces (~17 pN).
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C71 demonstrate through soft envelope simulations (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D) that allowing radial SPB movement increases spindle length modestly, but at physiologically realistic forces the length remains close to experimental measurements.

results.result: Progressive restriction in the model is motivated by monopolin complex and kinetochore compaction studies, though the model suggests additional molecules may contribute in fission yeast since monopolin is non-essential.
results.evaluation: Claims C147-C151 discuss the biological motivation for progressive restriction and note a discrepancy: monopolin is non-essential in fission yeast but progressive restriction is essential in the model. The speculation that other molecules contribute (C151) is reasonable but unproven, making this result uncertain.

results.result: The model exhibits ongoing kinetochore-MT attachment turnover and requires higher force-sensitivity than experimental measurements, representing discrepancies with experimental observations of stable metaphase biorientation.
results.evaluation: Claims C155, C157-C158 identify specific differences between model and experiment: the model shows ongoing attachment turnover and loss of biorientation, while experiments show stable metaphase biorientation. The model also requires higher force-sensitivity than measured experimentally. These are acknowledged limitations.

results.result: The model suggests that large spindle length fluctuations are more prominent in S. pombe than vertebrates because the small number of chromosomes and MTs in S. pombe makes force changes more significant.
results.evaluation: Claims C159-C160 present speculation about why large fluctuations occur in S. pombe but not vertebrates, based on the relative contribution of chromosome forces. While mechanistically reasonable, this is speculation without direct experimental validation in vertebrate systems.

results.result: The manuscript reviews established knowledge about spindle structure, kinetochore function, error correction mechanisms, and force balance models from prior literature.
results.evaluation: Claims C8-C26, C43, C45-C46, C48, C51, C58, C61, C64, C66, C75, C88-C90, C94, C101-C102, C114-C115, C117-C118, C123, C125-C126, and C130 cite prior literature to establish background knowledge. These are appropriately cited and represent accepted knowledge in the field.

results.result: The work provides a framework for testing spindle assembly mechanisms, though distinguishing direct from indirect effects of perturbations remains challenging.
results.evaluation: Claims C72, C116, and C167 make general statements about the utility and limitations of the modeling approach. These are supported by the demonstrated capabilities of the model and acknowledged challenges in interpretation.
